chapter_theme: After a payiram that says the book joins the householder's and the renouncer's codes and an invocation to the twenty-four, twenty verses count five to eight things under one predicate, moving between the household's giving and hospitality, the king's and minister's duties, and a Jain code of non-killing, truth and restraint; three verses close by setting the books of learning aside for conduct.

payiram.reading: The payiram says that Kanimethai, an ornament of good learning, gathered and told without lapse the books of virtue, joining the renouncer's code to the householder's, and mixed into the work the good way to release as well.
payiram.nuance: It names the book's plan rather than its title: two codes, the household and the renunciant, made one, with release added. கணிமேதை is the author's name, and அணிமேதை puns on it.

0.reading: The invocation says that one who tends and gives to the four, holding to the red feet praised by the twenty-four and following the four scriptures, will by nature leave the earth and live as lord over the gods.
0.nuance: அறுநால்வர் (six times four) is most likely the twenty-four Tirthankaras, which fits a Jain author, but the verse names no one. Who the four that are tended and given to are, and which four scriptures (நால் மறை) are meant, the verse does not say; our reading of a Jain fourfold canon and fourfold gift is a guess.

1.reading: The verse names six things (fame that has spread, wealth, eminence, valour in service, steadfast learning and liberality) and says, to a woman with flowered hair, that they are beauty only in those who walk the way of the scripture.
1.nuance: The goods named are worldly ones, but the closing line makes them beautiful only on the virtuous, so the verse ranks conduct over the goods it lists. நின்ற நிலை is taken with கல்வி as one item (steadfast learning); read apart, the list has seven.

items.claim: fame that has spread is a beauty in those who walk the scripture's way
wealth is a beauty in them
eminence, being spoken of highly, is a beauty in them
valour in service is a beauty in them
learning that stands firm is a beauty in them
liberality is a beauty in them

2.reading: The verse says that one who, though entitled to kill, does not kill, is not deluded by flesh, does no sharp torment, does not deceive and never swerves from his state rises above not only those on earth but those in the sky.
2.nuance: கொலையுரியான் கொல்லான் is taken as one item, one who has the right to kill (a king or a judge) and does not; read as two negatives (does not abet killing, does not kill) the verse has six items, the table's count. உரியான் is a positive form, which is why we read five.

items.claim: one who has the right to kill yet does not kill rises above earth and sky
one not deluded into eating flesh rises so
one who does no sharp torment rises so
one who does not deceive rises so
one who never swerves from his state rises so

3.reading: The verse sets easy things against hard ones: penance is easy and giving hard; [avoiding] waste is hard and falling into it easy; when blameless joy slips, joining with [grief] is easy, but wiping away that grief is hard.
3.nuance: Only the first pair is clear: the verse ranks giving as harder than penance. Line 1 ends in the obscure அரிதுக் கார்க்கேல், and the middle pairs are our construal of a damaged line; the six items follow the verse's easy/hard predicates.

items.claim: penance is easy
giving is hard
[avoiding] waste is hard
falling into it is easy
when blameless joy slips, falling in with its loss is easy
wiping away that grief is hard

4.reading: The verse names six practices (relieving distress, not scorning, not joining the base, relieving grief, giving up conduct blamed by all, and speech that those who see it desire) and says that where these are seen, the books of those who expound learning can be let go as unneeded.
4.nuance: The closing line sets conduct above book-learning: the list does what the books are for. கண்டவர் காமுறுஞ் சொல் is read as the sixth item and காணின் as 'if [these] are seen'.

items.claim: relieving others' distress makes the books of learning unneeded
not scorning others does so
not joining the company of the base does so
relieving grief does so
giving up conduct that all would blame does so
speech that those who meet it desire does so

5.reading: The verse says that one who is always his own companion, does not lie and makes his word true, claims nothing as 'mine', does not trust the words of women adorned like konrai blossoms and is not intoxicated, has what the support of other books would give.
5.nuance: Like verses 4 and 14, the verse ends by setting the books aside, but சாலும் பிறநூலின் சார்பு can mean either that he needs no other book or that he is enough to be one; தனக்கென்றும் ஓர்பாங்கன் may instead mean one who keeps a single friend. The distrust of women's words is a gender rule of the period.

items.claim: one who is ever his own companion has what other books give
one who does not lie and makes his word true has it
one who claims nothing as his own has it
one who does not trust the words of adorned women has it
one who is not intoxicated has it

norm.note: a rule of the period that a man of virtue does not trust women's words

6.reading: The verse says, to a woman with bamboo-like shoulders, that one who has self-restraint, a gentle nature, giving, patience, and a door shut to falsehood and to flesh is fit to be called a mother to all living beings.
6.nuance: மறையுடைமை governs both பொய்ம்மை and புலால், so the last two items share one predicate of keeping them out; the six are counted that way. The reward is not heaven but a title: mother to every life.

items.claim: self-restraint makes one a mother to all lives
a gentle nature does so
giving does so
patience does so
keeping falsehood shut out does so
keeping flesh shut out does so

7.reading: The verse says that if a man, putting away harsh words, gives to everyone sweet speech, warm mingling, a place to sit and good food, the gods in the sky will hasten to receive him as their guest every day.
7.nuance: The four gifts are graded from words to food, and the fifth item is a removal (harsh words) that frames them all.

items.claim: sweet speech to all wins the gods' welcome
cordial mingling does so
giving a place does so
giving good food does so
putting away harsh words does so

8.reading: The verse says that one who does not consent to killing, does not kill, relieves the sickness of the afflicted, does not fall into folly, and enters the excellent books of the excellent, studying them widely, will be raised by those who raise men, who come close to him.
8.nuance: ஆக்குமவர் ஆக்கும் அணைந்து is obscure: 'those who make [men great]' may be the gods or the virtuous. Consenting to a killing is counted as an act separate from killing.

items.claim: one who does not consent to killing is raised up
one who does not kill is raised up
one who relieves the sickness of the afflicted is raised up
one who does not fall into folly is raised up
one who enters widely into the books of the excellent is raised up

9.reading: The verse says that those who, not rating the learned only by their learning nor their kin only by kinship, give food, shelter and clothing to the destitute will live as learned men, practised in it.
9.nuance: The reward is a paradox: giving, not study, makes one a பண்டிதர். Lines 1-2 are hard to construe; we read them as giving without regard to the receiver's learning or kinship.

items.claim: not rating the learned only by their learning makes one a learned man
not weighing kin by kinship does so
giving food to the destitute does so
giving them shelter does so
giving them clothing does so

10.reading: The verse sets the wealth of subjects under a just sceptre against the ruin of subjects under a cruel and worthless one and the work of a cruel sceptre's ministers, and says that 'we' cannot know these fully for not knowing anything at all.
10.nuance: Lines 3-4 (அறியலம்ஒன்(று) ஆற்ற எனைத்தும் அறியாமை யான்) are obscure; the speaker's disclaimer may be ironic, or the sense may be that a ruler who cannot do even one thing fully cannot know these. The three items are clear, the predicate is not.

items.claim: the wealth of subjects under a just sceptre is set out
the ruin of subjects under a cruel sceptre is set against it
the work of a cruel sceptre's ministers is named with it

11.reading: The verse says that one who has set out to cut desire does not slacken, that cutting the desire for those five fully is enough, and that one who does not cut it is tossed about by the five elephants and goes sullen into the hole.
11.nuance: The verse does not list its five; ஐங்களிறு (five elephants) makes them the senses. புழை, the narrow hole, is most likely rebirth. The three items are the verse's three states of desire, not a counted list.

items.claim: one who sets out to cut desire does not slacken
cutting desire for the five fully is enough
one who does not cut it is tossed by the five elephants into the hole

12.reading: The verse names five places (the killing ground, the ground where men gamble with strips, the place of torment, the ground where war elephants are trained, and the place where the three circlings are made) and says it is good neither to desire them nor to look at them.
12.nuance: Even looking is barred: the rule reaches past doing violence to watching it. வார்குத்து and முச்சாரிகை are rare words; the latter is perhaps the wheeling of horses or elephants in drill.

items.claim: it is good not to desire or look at the killing ground
nor at the place where men gamble
nor at the place of torment
nor at the ground where war elephants are trained
nor at the place where the three circlings are made

13.reading: The verse says that not sowing, not eating, not bathing, not fretting greatly, conquering so as to inspire awe, and not plucking out are, on inspection, the six marks kept by those who hold to the books and stand in their portion.
13.nuance: Our division of line 2 (உட்குடைத்தா வென்று, களையாமை) is doubtful. Read as a Jain ascetic's code, not sowing and not weeding would avoid harm to life in the soil, and not bathing is a known renunciant rule, the reverse of the householder's bathing rules elsewhere in this group.

items.claim: not sowing is a mark of the ascetic
fasting is one
not bathing is one
not fretting greatly is one
conquering so as to inspire awe is one
not plucking or weeding is one

14.reading: The verse says, to a woman with fish-like eyes, that for one who does not lie, has put away flesh and toddy, does no evil, does not join the base and does not revile, the books are, on reflection, always beside the point.
14.nuance: Flesh and toddy are joined by ஒடு but counted as two, giving six. The predicate (அயல அயலவாம் நூல்) puts the books outside such a man, the third time in the chapter conduct replaces the book.

items.claim: one who does not lie has no need of the books
one who has put away flesh has none
one who has put away toddy has none
one who does no evil has none
one who does not join the base has none
one who does not revile has none

15.reading: The verse calls good five things: not being angry with those dear as one's eyes, joining the company of the learned, not clinging to those whose speech is like music, not letting a precious secret slip to those whose words are melodious, and relieving the distress of the poor even a little.
15.nuance: Items 3 and 4 both guard against sweet speakers: one forbids attachment, the other forbids trusting them with a secret. பண்போல் கிளவியார் may be women, but the word does not say so.

items.claim: not being angry with those dear as one's eyes is good
joining the company of the learned is good
not clinging to those of music-like speech is good
not letting a precious secret slip to sweet talkers is good
relieving the poor's distress, even a little, is good

16.reading: The verse says that if a man draws near to renunciants, gives to those who have not renounced, speaks well of the dead, and honours and tends the kin the dead leave behind, his life is sweet and without ruin.
16.nuance: Four items, not six: the verse pairs those who renounced with those who did not, then the dead with their kin. இறந்தார்க்கு இனிய இசைத்தல் may also mean rites for the dead.

items.claim: drawing near to renunciants makes life sweet
giving to those who have not renounced does so
speaking well of the dead does so
honouring and tending the kin the dead leave does so

17.reading: The verse names what makes a trusted minister: guarding the people, resolve, strength in learning, secret counsel, the power to keep off sloth, and, guarding the crown and discerning in smell, taste and hearing, keeping the company of the good.
17.nuance: Six nominal items are counted; முடியோம்பி நாற்றம் சுவைகேள்வி is read as a phrase qualifying the last, which is doubtful. கூடம் may be secret counsel or stratagem. The last line (தேற்றானேல் தேறும்) may mean that even untested, such a man is to be trusted.

items.claim: guarding the people marks a trusted minister
resolve does so
strength in learning does so
secret counsel does so
the power to keep off sloth does so
keeping the company of the good does so

18.reading: The verse says that if a king guards against sensual indulgence, waste of wealth, deer-hunting, evil toddy, gambling that brings grief, harsh force of words, cruel and wrathful punishment, and lack of restraint, other kings will have no wrath that can destroy him.
18.nuance: The first seven items match the old list of a king's seven vices (women, hunting, drink, dice, harsh words, harsh punishment, waste); அடங்காமை closes them as their sum. Eight items against the table's six.

items.claim: guarding against sensual indulgence keeps a king safe from rivals
guarding against waste of wealth does so
guarding against deer-hunting does so
guarding against evil toddy does so
guarding against gambling that brings grief does so
guarding against harsh force of words does so
guarding against cruel, wrathful punishment does so
guarding against lack of restraint does so

19.reading: The verse names as belonging to one greater than a king: not killing, not causing killing, not lying, not going after another's wife, not joining the base, being deaf to secrets told, and dumb to evil speech.
19.nuance: Seven items against the table's six. இறையில் பெரியான் can be 'one greater than a king' or 'the great one without fault'; either way the list is a measure of greatness.

items.claim: not killing belongs to one greater than a king
not causing killing does
not lying does
not going after another's wife does
not joining the base does
being deaf to secrets that are told does
being dumb to evil speech does

20.reading: The verse says that one who does not trust the words of women with lightning-slim waists, does not heed desire, does not rage in vain, does not kill, delights in giving even when it is like cutting off a limb, and has cut hatred out of himself has no equal even in heaven.
20.nuance: The giving that cuts like a limb is the hardest gift, which recalls verse 3's ranking of giving above penance. The distrust of women's words repeats verse 5's gender rule.

items.claim: one who does not trust the words of slim-waisted women has no equal in heaven
one who does not heed desire has none
one who does not rage in vain has none
one who does not kill has none
one who delights in giving even when it cuts like a limb has none
one who has cut out hatred has none

norm.note: a rule of the period that the virtuous man does not trust women's words

links.note: Kural 260 says all creatures worship the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; Elathi 2 says the one who has the right to kill and does not, and is not deluded by flesh, rises above gods as well as men.
links.teaches: The pair shows the Jain ethics raising the stake: the Kural's worship by the spared creatures becomes rank above the gods, and the abstention counts most in the one who has the power to kill.
links.list_adds: It puts non-killing and refusing flesh first in a list with not tormenting, not deceiving and not swerving, so the two abstentions of 260 become the head of a five-part code rather than its whole.

links.note: Kural 263 chides householders who have forgotten penance in providing for renunciants; Elathi 3 says outright that penance is easy and giving is hard.
links.teaches: Read with 263, the verse reverses the ranking the Kural's chiding implies: if giving is the harder task, the householder who gives instead of doing penance has chosen the steeper road.
links.list_adds: It sets penance and giving as the first of several easy-hard pairs, so the ranking of the two is stated as a rule of difficulty rather than left to a rhetorical question.

links.note: Kural 391 says learn flawlessly and then stand by what is learned; Elathi 4 says that where six kinds of kindly conduct are seen, the books of learning may be let go.
links.teaches: The Kural makes conduct the completion of learning, while Elathi makes it a substitute: together they show two orders, learning that leads to conduct and conduct that makes the books unnecessary.
links.list_adds: It names the six acts that do the books' work (relieving distress, not scorning, shunning the base, relieving grief, avoiding blame, desired speech), so the conduct that replaces learning is specified, which 391 leaves general.

links.note: Kural 30 calls those who wear cool kindness toward every living being the அந்தணர்; Elathi 6 calls one who has six possessions a mother to all living beings.
links.teaches: Both give a title for care toward every creature, but Elathi grounds it in six restraints, keeping out lies and flesh among them, so universal care is built from abstentions, not only from a cool temper.
links.list_adds: It breaks the single quality of 30 into six possessions, two of them shutting out falsehood and flesh, and gives the outcome a mother's name instead of a status word.

links.note: Kural 86 says the host who tends the guest and watches for the next becomes a guest of the gods; Elathi 7 says the gods hasten to receive as guest one who gives sweet speech, mingling, a seat and good food without harsh words.
links.teaches: The couplet promises the reward and Elathi spells out the hospitality that earns it, so the pair shows the heavenly reciprocity resting on manner of speech as much as on food.
links.list_adds: It itemises hospitality into speech, mingling, a seat and food, with harsh words removed, a grading from word to meal that 86 does not make.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 69 counts the one who agreed to a killing among five who share its sin; Elathi 8 opens its list with not consenting and not killing as two separate acts.
links.teaches: Together the two Jain lists show consent treated as its own act of killing: one assigns it a share of the sin, the other makes refusing it a virtue in its own right.

links.note: Kural 226 says relieving the hunger of the destitute (அற்றார்) is where one should store wealth; Elathi 9 says giving food, shelter and clothing to the destitute (அற்றார்கட்கு) makes one live as a learned man.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the gift a bank for wealth and Elathi makes it a source of wisdom, so the same act toward the destitute is repaid in two different coins.
links.list_adds: It widens the gift from food to food, shelter and clothing and adds giving without regard to the receiver's learning or kinship, which 226 does not mention.

links.note: Kural 367 says that if one cuts desire fully, the deeds that do not fail come; Elathi 11 echoes it (அவாஅறுப்பின் ஆற்ற) and adds the fate of one who does not cut it.
links.teaches: The near-verbatim echo shows Elathi reading the couplet and supplying its other half: what 367 leaves unsaid, the failure to cut desire, is rebirth under the five senses.
links.list_adds: It sets the one who cuts desire beside the one who does not, so the couplet's promise becomes one branch of a choice with a stated penalty.

links.note: Kural 24 guards the five with the goad of firmness, implying elephants without naming them; Elathi 11 names the five elephants (ஐங்களிறு) that toss the one who does not cut desire.
links.teaches: Elathi makes explicit the elephants the couplet only implies, and shows what happens when the goad is missing: the senses carry their rider into the hole of rebirth.
links.list_adds: It turns the goad image into a narrative of failure, the rider tossed by the five, which the couplet's image of control does not show.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 68 says long bathing at a ghat does not remove the blemish; Elathi 13 counts not bathing (ஆடாமை, on our reading) among the six marks of ascetics.
links.teaches: On this reading the two Jain lists move from denying bathing any cleansing power to making its refusal a mark of the renunciant, the reverse of the bathing rules of the Acharakkovai.

links.note: Kural 834 calls the greatest fool one who studies, understands and teaches but does not restrain himself; Elathi 14 says that for one who keeps six restraints the books are beside the point.
links.teaches: Held together the two state the same principle from opposite ends: learning without restraint is folly, and restraint without learning already has what the books are for.
links.list_adds: It names the restraints (no lying, no flesh, no toddy, no evil, no base company, no reviling) that 834 leaves as a single self-restraint, and puts flesh and toddy among them.

links.note: Verse 4 lets the books go where six kindly acts are seen; verse 14 puts the books outside one who keeps six abstentions.
links.teaches: The repeated close shows the chapter treating conduct over books as a refrain, and the two lists divide that conduct into acts of kindness (4) and acts of refusal (14).

links.note: Thirikadugam 55 names a friendship that does not keep a precious secret (அருமறை) as one of three spies; Elathi 15 counts not letting a precious secret slip to sweet talkers as good.
links.teaches: Together they show the secret's danger from both sides: Thirikadugam names the friend who leaks it as a spy, and Elathi locates the leak in the listener's trust of pleasant speech.

links.note: Kural 42 makes the householder the support of those who renounced, those who have nothing and the dead; Elathi 16 names drawing near to renunciants, giving to those who have not renounced, speaking well of the dead and tending their kin.
links.teaches: The verse reads like a gloss on 42: it keeps the three figures and turns the dead into the living kin they leave, so the householder's duty to the dead becomes care of a household.
links.list_adds: It turns the three dependants of 42 into four acts and adds the kin of the dead, so the list says how the support is given, not only to whom.

links.note: Kural 632 names a minister excellent in resolve, guarding the people, learning and labour; Elathi 17 names guarding the people, resolve and strength in learning, then adds secret counsel, keeping off sloth and good company.
links.teaches: The two share three of their qualities in near-identical words (குடி, வன்கண், கற்றல்/நூல்வன்மை), and Elathi's additions show a minister judged also by the company he keeps and by his secrecy.
links.list_adds: It adds secret counsel and good company to the Kural's core, so ministerial fitness extends from capacity to discretion and associations.

links.note: Kural 920 makes double-minded women, liquor and dice the company of those Fortune has abandoned; Elathi 18 lists indulgence, waste, hunting, toddy, gambling, harsh words, harsh punishment and unrestraint as what a king must guard against.
links.teaches: The couplet's three ruinous companions reappear inside Elathi's longer list of the king's vices, which shows the Kural's general warning taken up into a royal code where it secures the kingdom against rivals.
links.list_adds: It places the Kural's three vices among the seven of kingship (adding hunting, waste, harsh words and harsh punishment) and closes with unrestraint as their sum, carrying the warning into the king's domain.

links.note: Naladiyar 158 says one deaf to others' secrets, blind to a neighbour's wife and dumb in evil backbiting needs no teaching of virtue; Elathi 19 names the same deafness to secrets and dumbness to evil speech, with not killing and not lying, as the marks of one greater than a king.
links.teaches: The shared images of deafness and dumbness show the two Jain works using one figure for restraint, and Elathi's addition of non-killing turns the Naladiyar's man who needs no teaching into a rank above kings.
links.list_adds: It sets the Naladiyar's restraints of the senses after non-killing, not causing killing and not lying, so sense restraint is ranked behind non-violence and truth in a seven-part list.

links.note: Purananuru 43 recalls the Chola ancestor who entered the scales for a dove; Elathi 20 praises one who delights in giving even when it is like cutting off a limb.
links.teaches: Read with Puram 43, Elathi's simile carries the memory of the king who gave his own flesh: the heroic deed of an ancestor becomes the measure of ordinary giving for anyone.

source_issues: Verse 17: show flags that the site's text lacks line 1.
Verse 16 line 1: துறவார்(கு) is likely துறவார்க்கு with the க் lost.
Verse 3 line 1: அரிதுக் கார்க்கேல் is obscure and may be corrupt; the middle easy/hard pairs are uncertain.
Verse 10 lines 3-4: the predicate (அறியலம்ஒன்(று) ஆற்ற எனைத்தும் அறியாமை யான்) is hard to construe.
Verse 13 line 2: the division of உட்குடைத்தா வென்று is doubtful.
